newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Western ad agencies flourish in Czech Republic.
newsitem.headline: Western ad agencies flourish in Czech Republic.

text.p: In seven years the Czech advertising industry has raced headlong into capitalism.
After emerging from a communist era that permitted only two, state-controlled advertising agencies, the Czech Republic now has 3,000 advertising agencies in a country of just 10 million people.

But most agencies are small, cottage-industry operations fighting for survival. The bulk of the business is controlled by Western agenices, brought in by large, multi-national companies keen to introduce consumer goods to new markets.
The top 10 agencies control 50 percent of the Czech advertising business. And within the top 20 agencies, only two or three are 100 percent locally owned.

Similarly, most of the advertising business is generated by Western companies. "In the top 20 advertisers only three are Czech companies," Josef Havelka, managing director for Leo Burnett Advertising in the Czech Republic, said in an interview on Thursday.

Leo Burnett, a privately held agency based in Chicago, generates half of its business from international clients. In fact, Havelka said in the entire republic there are only 10 to 15 Czech companies that are significant advertisers.

"There are some Czech companies that are spending, but they spend very little," he said. Although many Czech companies bloomed in the aftermath of communism, few have had the capital to compete with multi-national companies.
"Their strategy is not to build brands but to run price wars," Havelka said. As a result, Czech companies tend to have slender profit margins and lack funds to reinvest in business.

Most of the advertising is done by multi-national companies such as Procter & Gamble -- the world's largest advertiser, Unilever and Nestle. They work with ad agencies with whom they have had longstanding relationships throughout the world.

As a result, most major Western ad agencies are represented in the country, including BBDO, owned by Abbott Mead Vickers Plc and the largest agency in the country, Omnicom's DDB and TBWA agencies, WPP Group Plc's Ogilvy and Mather, Young and Rubicam, and Darcy Masius Benton & Bowles.

But being successful takes more than just money. Although many companies were quick to begin advertising after the 1989 Velvet Revolution ushered in capitalism, they learned that advertising could hinder rather than help sales.

Under communism shortages of consumer goods were commonplace, making advertised goods suspect in a world where demand typically outstripped the supply of desired products. In addition, the state-controlled advertising business had relied on a heavily factual approach, and consumers did not know how to relate the lifestyle adverts favoured in the West.
Initially, advertisers were simply taking ads already running in Western countries and translating them into Czech.

"Most of the smarter companies have learned this is not the best way to do it," Havelka said. What the more sophisticated companies now do is use the basic strategy they have in the West and use it to create new ads tailored to the Czech market.

Part of the recipe for success lies in having locally hired staff who understand Czech culture, said Havelka, a Czech native who left the country at age 16 and returned five years ago after living in Germany and the U.S.

The industry, however, remains highly competitive. Newer, smaller agencies have been offering to cut the typical 15 percent commission that agenices receive on a client's media spend to as low as three percent, Havelka said.
The advertising business is continuing to grow, roughly at a rate twice that of the country's gross domestic product. Continued growth, however, depends on the overall economy.
"The optimistic view here is that it will follow the East Asian pattern of growth for emerging markets," said Havelka. "The pessimistic view is there could be a change in government."
